insights.body: Teman (36:11) became known for its wise men. Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite.

insights.title: Before any king in Israel
insights.body: These are the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel (36:31). Edom had kings long before Israel did, a detail that hints the final writer knew of Israel's monarchy.

insights.title: Brothers and nations
insights.body: Israel and Edom, brothers, become neighbors and often enemies. Obadiah and Malachi deal with this long rivalry.

insights.title: Not chosen, still blessed
insights.body: Esau wasn't the line of promise, yet God blessed him. How does God's generosity to others shape the way you see them?

37.summary: Jacob loves Joseph more than his brothers and gives him a special robe; Joseph dreams that his family will bow to him, and his brothers hate him; sent to check on them, he is thrown into a pit and sold to traders bound for Egypt; the brothers dip his robe in goat's blood, and Jacob mourns, believing him dead.
37.lookfor: Notice the favoritism, the dreams, and Reuben's and Judah's different roles.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: Jacob's favorite son, 17 years old.

names.name: Dothan
names.gloss: A town north of Shechem on a trade route to Egypt.

names.name: Reuben
names.gloss: The oldest brother, who tried to save Joseph.

names.name: Judah
names.gloss: Who proposed selling Joseph.

names.name: Ishmaelites
names.gloss: Traders, also called Midianites, carrying goods to Egypt.

names.name: Potiphar
names.gloss: An Egyptian official, captain of Pharaoh's guard.

insights.title: The coat
insights.body: Jacob makes Joseph a long robe with sleeves (37:3), traditionally a coat of many colors. It marked status, not work clothes; it signaled the favorite as heir.

insights.title: Dreams
insights.body: Sheaves bowing, then sun, moon and eleven stars bowing (37:7-9). Joseph tells them unwisely; the dreams come true, but not as anyone expects.

insights.title: Favoritism repeats
insights.body: Isaac favored Esau, Rebekah favored Jacob, and now Jacob favors Rachel's son (37:3). Favoritism again breeds hatred.

insights.title: The pit was empty
insights.body: They threw him into a pit; the pit was empty, with no water in it (37:24). Then they sat down to eat bread. Callousness beside cruelty.

insights.title: Twenty pieces of silver
insights.body: Joseph is sold for twenty pieces of silver (37:28), about the price of a young slave in that era, as records from the time suggest.

insights.title: A goat and a garment
insights.body: The brothers dip Joseph's robe in goat's blood to fool Jacob (37:31-33). Jacob once used a goat and his brother's garments to fool his own father.

insights.title: Sold into Egypt
insights.body: The story ends with Joseph sold to Potiphar in Egypt (37:36). It looks like the end of his dreams, but it is the road to their fulfillment.

insights.title: Jealousy
insights.body: The brothers' jealousy grew from words to hatred to violence. Where is jealousy growing in you, and how could you stop it early?

38.summary: Judah leaves his brothers, marries a Canaanite, and has three sons; the first two die after wronging their widow Tamar, and Judah withholds the third; Tamar disguises herself, conceives by Judah, and when he condemns her, she produces his seal, cord and staff; Judah admits she is more righteous, and she bears twins, Perez and Zerah.
38.lookfor: Notice why this story interrupts Joseph's, and Judah's confession.

names.name: Judah
names.gloss: Jacob's fourth son.

names.name: Tamar
names.gloss: Judah's daughter-in-law, twice widowed.

names.name: Er
names.gloss: Judah's firstborn, who was wicked and died.

names.name: Onan
names.gloss: Judah's second son, who refused to give Tamar a child.

names.name: Shelah
names.gloss: Judah's third son, withheld from Tamar.

names.name: Perez
names.gloss: One of Tamar's twins; ancestor of David.

insights.title: An interruption
insights.body: Right after Judah sells Joseph, the story turns to Judah's failures (38:1). It sets up his transformation: the man who sold a brother will later offer himself for one.

insights.title: Levirate marriage
insights.body: When a man died childless, his brother was to have a son with the widow to carry on the dead man's name (38:8). Later law formalized this. Onan's refusal was selfish exploitation.

insights.title: Seal, cord and staff
insights.body: Tamar asks for Judah's seal, cord and staff as a pledge (38:18), like leaving your ID card. The cylinder seal on a cord was a man's signature.

insights.title: More righteous than I
insights.body: Faced with the evidence, Judah says, she is more righteous than I, because I didn't give her to my son Shelah (38:26). His first recorded confession.

insights.title: In Jesus' family tree
insights.body: Tamar is the first of four women Matthew names in Jesus' genealogy, along with Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba (38:29). God's line runs through scandal and outsiders.

insights.title: Perez
insights.body: Perez means breach or breaking out, because he broke out first (38:29). From Perez come Boaz, Jesse, David and Jesus.

insights.title: Grace through failure
insights.body: God's promise of a royal line (49:10) runs through this sordid story. Grace works through human mess.

insights.title: Admitting wrong
insights.body: Judah could have hidden his guilt but owned it publicly. Is there something you need to admit, as Judah did?

39.summary: In Egypt Yahweh is with Joseph, and Potiphar puts him in charge of his house; Potiphar's wife repeatedly tries to seduce him, and he refuses; she accuses him falsely, and he is thrown into prison, where Yahweh is with him again and the warden puts him in charge.
39.lookfor: Notice the repeated phrase "Yahweh was with Joseph," and Joseph's reason for refusing.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: A Hebrew slave in Egypt.

names.name: Potiphar
names.gloss: Captain of Pharaoh's guard, Joseph's master.

names.name: Egypt
names.gloss: The land where Joseph was a slave.

insights.title: Yahweh was with Joseph
insights.body: The phrase Yahweh was with Joseph frames the chapter (39:2, 39:21, 39:23). God's presence doesn't prevent slavery or prison but is with him in both.

insights.title: An overseer
insights.body: Potiphar left everything in Joseph's hand and didn't concern himself with anything except the food he ate (39:6). Egyptian households of officials had stewards over property and servants; Egyptians may have kept food matters to themselves.

insights.title: Against God
insights.body: How can I do this great wickedness and sin against God? (39:9). Joseph sees sin as betrayal of God, not just of his master.

insights.title: Day after day
insights.body: She spoke to Joseph day by day, and he refused (39:10). Temptation came repeatedly; faithfulness was a daily choice.

insights.title: He fled
insights.body: He left his garment in her hand and ran outside (39:12). Paul's advice to Timothy: flee youthful lusts.

insights.title: Another garment
insights.body: Again a garment is used to lie about Joseph (39:16), as his brothers used his robe. Twice stripped, twice falsely portrayed.

insights.title: Faithful in prison
insights.body: Unjustly imprisoned, Joseph serves faithfully, and the warden trusts him with everything (39:22). Faithfulness in small places prepares for great ones.

insights.title: Unfair outcomes
insights.body: Joseph did right and was punished. How do you keep trusting God when doing right costs you?

40.summary: In prison Joseph cares for Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, who have troubling dreams; Joseph says interpretations belong to God and interprets them: the cupbearer will be restored and the baker executed in three days; both come true, but the cupbearer forgets Joseph.
40.lookfor: Notice Joseph's concern for the prisoners, and the last sad verse.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: A prisoner in charge of other prisoners.

names.name: Pharaoh
names.gloss: Egypt's king, whose officials offended him.

insights.title: Cupbearer and baker
insights.body: The chief cupbearer and chief baker controlled the king's drink and food (40:1-2). These were posts of trust and closeness to the king, since poisoning was a constant danger. Nehemiah later held the same role.

insights.title: Why so sad?
insights.body: Joseph sees their faces and asks, why do you look so sad today? (40:7). In his own suffering, he notices others'.

insights.title: Interpretations belong to God
insights.body: Don't interpretations belong to God? Please tell it to me (40:8). Egypt had professional dream interpreters with manuals; Joseph points to God.

insights.title: Lift up your head
insights.body: Pharaoh will lift up your head (40:13, 40:19), a pun: for the cupbearer it means restoration; for the baker, beheading.

insights.title: Remember me
insights.body: Joseph asks, remember me when it goes well with you (40:14). He was kidnapped and imprisoned for nothing. The thief on the cross makes a similar request of Jesus.

insights.title: Forgotten
insights.body: Yet the chief cupbearer didn't remember Joseph, but forgot him (40:23). Two more years pass (41:1). Waiting is part of God's plan.

insights.title: Forgotten by people
insights.body: Joseph was forgotten by the one he helped. When have you felt forgotten, and how did God meet you there?

41.summary: Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones and seven good ears of grain swallowed by seven thin ones; no one can interpret until the cupbearer remembers Joseph, who explains seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine and advises storing grain; Pharaoh makes Joseph ruler over Egypt at thirty, and he marries and has two sons.
41.lookfor: Notice how quickly Joseph rises, and the names he gives his sons.

names.name: Pharaoh
names.gloss: Egypt's king, troubled by dreams.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: Raised from prison to second in Egypt.

names.name: Zaphenath-Paneah
names.gloss: Joseph's Egyptian name.

names.name: Asenath
names.gloss: Joseph's Egyptian wife, daughter of a priest of On.

names.name: Manasseh
names.gloss: Joseph's first son; the name sounds like making forget.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: Joseph's second son; the name sounds like fruitful.

insights.title: Cows from the Nile
insights.body: Cows come up out of the river (41:2). Egypt's wealth depended on the Nile's yearly flood; cattle grazing in its reeds were a picture of plenty, and failed floods meant famine.

insights.title: Shaved and changed
insights.body: Joseph shaves and changes his clothes before seeing Pharaoh (41:14). Egyptians were clean-shaven; Hebrews wore beards. He becomes presentable to an Egyptian court.

insights.title: It is not in me
insights.body: It isn't in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace (41:16). After thirteen years of suffering, Joseph's first words to the king point away from himself.

insights.title: Signet, linen and gold
insights.body: Pharaoh gives Joseph his signet ring, fine linen and a gold chain, and has people cry bow the knee before him (41:42-43). Egyptian paintings show officials installed this way.

insights.title: Thirty years old
insights.body: Joseph was thirty when he stood before Pharaoh (41:46), thirteen years after being sold. David began to reign at thirty; Jesus began his ministry at about thirty.

insights.title: Forget and fruitful
insights.body: Manasseh: God has made me forget all my toil. Ephraim: God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction (41:51-52). Healing and fruitfulness, both credited to God.

insights.title: Feeding the world
insights.body: All the earth came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph (41:57). Abraham's family begins to bless the nations, as promised.

insights.title: Fruitful in affliction
insights.body: Joseph found fruitfulness in the land of his suffering. Where might God be making you fruitful in a hard place?

42.summary: Famine drives Jacob to send ten sons to Egypt for grain, keeping Benjamin home; Joseph recognizes his brothers, who bow to him, but they don't recognize him; he accuses them of spying, jails Simeon, and demands they bring Benjamin; the brothers see their trouble as payback for Joseph, and find their money returned in their sacks.
42.lookfor: Notice the dreams coming true, the brothers' guilty consciences, and Joseph's hidden tears.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: Governor of Egypt, unrecognized by his brothers.

names.name: Benjamin
names.gloss: Joseph's full brother, kept at home.

names.name: Simeon
names.gloss: The brother held in prison.

names.name: Reuben
names.gloss: Who reminds them he warned against harming Joseph.

names.name: Canaan
names.gloss: Jacob's home, stricken by famine.

insights.title: The dreams come true
insights.body: Joseph's brothers bowed down to him with their faces to the earth, and Joseph remembered the dreams (42:6-9). Twenty years later, the sheaves bow.

insights.title: Why the test?
insights.body: Joseph speaks roughly and tests them (42:7). Not revenge, but to see whether they've changed: will they abandon another brother as they abandoned him?

insights.title: Guilty consciences
insights.body: The brothers say to each other, we are certainly guilty concerning our brother; we saw his distress when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen (42:21). Twenty years of buried guilt surface.

insights.title: He turned away and wept
insights.body: Joseph understood them, for he spoke through an interpreter, and he turned away and wept (42:23-24). The stern governor is a grieving brother.

insights.title: Money in the sacks
insights.body: They find their money returned in their sacks and their hearts fail them: what has God done to us? (42:28). Returned money could make them look like thieves.

insights.title: All these things are against me
insights.body: Jacob says, all these things are against me (42:36). In fact, all these things are working for him. Paul says God works all things for good.

insights.title: Seeds of change
insights.body: Reuben offers his own sons as pledge for Benjamin's safety (42:37). The brothers are beginning to change; Judah will go further.

insights.title: Buried guilt
insights.body: The brothers' guilt resurfaced after twenty years. Is there something from your past that God is inviting you to face?

43.summary: As the famine continues, Judah persuades Jacob to send Benjamin, offering himself as surety; the brothers return to Egypt with gifts and double money; Joseph invites them to his house, releases Simeon, weeps privately at seeing Benjamin, and feasts with them, giving Benjamin five times as much.
43.lookfor: Notice Judah's pledge, and how Joseph seats and serves his brothers.

names.name: Judah
names.gloss: Who offers to bear the blame if Benjamin is lost.

names.name: Benjamin
names.gloss: Rachel's younger son.

names.name: Israel
names.gloss: Jacob, reluctantly releasing Benjamin.

names.name: Simeon
names.gloss: Released from prison.

insights.title: I will be surety
insights.body: Judah tells his father, I will be surety for him; if I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever (43:9). The brother who sold Joseph now pledges himself for Benjamin.

insights.title: A gift for the governor
insights.body: Jacob sends balm, honey, spices, myrrh, pistachio nuts and almonds (43:11), products of Canaan that Egypt lacked. The same goods the traders carried when Joseph was sold.

insights.title: If I am bereaved
insights.body: Jacob says, if I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved (43:14). Resigned trust: he lets go of Benjamin and entrusts the outcome to God Almighty.

insights.title: He sought a place to weep
insights.body: Seeing Benjamin, Joseph was deeply moved, went into his room and wept, then washed his face and came out (43:30-31). He has to hide his love for now.

insights.title: Separate tables
insights.body: Joseph eats separately, the Egyptians separately, and the brothers separately, because Egyptians wouldn't eat with Hebrews (43:32). Egyptian records show disdain for foreign herdsmen.

insights.title: Five times as much
insights.body: Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs (43:34). Joseph tests whether they'll resent the favorite son, as they once resented him.

insights.title: Seated in order
insights.body: The brothers are seated from oldest to youngest, and they look at one another in amazement (43:33). Someone here knows them far better than they realize.

insights.title: Taking responsibility
insights.body: Judah offered himself in place of another. Whose burden could you take responsibility for out of love?

44.summary: Joseph has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack, then sends his steward to accuse the brothers of theft; the cup is found and they return in despair; Joseph says only Benjamin must stay as a slave, but Judah steps forward and pleads to take Benjamin's place for his father's sake.
44.lookfor: Notice the final test, and Judah's speech, the longest in Genesis.

names.name: Benjamin
names.gloss: In whose sack the cup is found.

names.name: Judah
names.gloss: Who offers to become a slave in Benjamin's place.

insights.title: A cup for divination
insights.body: Isn't this the cup my lord drinks from and uses for divination? (44:5). Egyptians read omens from liquids in a cup; Joseph uses the claim to raise the stakes.

insights.title: The final test
insights.body: Joseph offers them a way out: only the guilty one, Benjamin, must stay; the rest may go home in peace (44:17). Will they abandon Rachel's other son, as they abandoned Joseph?

insights.title: God has found out our iniquity
insights.body: Judah says, God has found out the iniquity of your servants (44:16). He isn't confessing to stealing the cup but to the old sin against Joseph.

insights.title: His life is bound up
insights.body: Judah explains that his father's life is bound up in the boy's life (44:30). He speaks with compassion for the father he once deceived.

insights.title: Let me stay instead
insights.body: Let your servant stay as a slave instead of the boy, and let the boy go up with his brothers (44:33). The brother who sold one brother into slavery now offers himself as a slave for another. Many see a picture of Christ, from Judah's tribe, who took our place.

insights.title: Tearing clothes
insights.body: The brothers tear their clothes (44:13), as Jacob tore his at the news of Joseph. Now they share their father's grief.

insights.title: Surety
insights.body: Your servant became surety for the boy (44:32). The word means to stand as guarantee, taking on someone else's debt. Hebrews calls Jesus the surety of a better covenant.

insights.title: Changed
insights.body: Judah was a different man from the one who sold Joseph. How has God changed you over the years?

45.summary: Overwhelmed, Joseph sends everyone out and reveals himself, weeping so loudly that the Egyptians hear; he tells his terrified brothers not to be distressed, because God sent him ahead to preserve life; he sends them to bring Jacob to Goshen, and Jacob, hearing Joseph is alive, revives.
45.lookfor: Notice how many times Joseph says God sent me, and his advice not to quarrel on the way.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: Who finally reveals himself.

names.name: Goshen
names.gloss: Fertile land in the eastern Nile delta.

names.name: Pharaoh
names.gloss: Who welcomes Joseph's family.

insights.title: I am Joseph
insights.body: I am Joseph! Does my father still live? (45:3). The brothers are terrified and can't answer. His first question is about his father.

insights.title: God sent me
insights.body: Don't be grieved or angry with yourselves that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life (45:5). Joseph says God sent me three times (45:5, 45:7, 45:8). He doesn't excuse their sin but sees God's bigger purpose.

insights.title: A great deliverance
insights.body: God sent me to preserve for you a remnant on the earth and to save you alive by a great deliverance (45:7). The family of promise is rescued, and through them, the world's future.

insights.title: Father to Pharaoh
insights.body: God made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of his house and ruler of Egypt (45:8). Father was an Egyptian title for a high adviser.

insights.title: Don't quarrel on the way
insights.body: As he sends them off, Joseph says, see that you don't quarrel on the way (45:24). He knows his brothers well; blame could start flying.

insights.title: His spirit revived
insights.body: When Jacob saw the wagons Joseph sent, his spirit revived (45:27). Israel said, it is enough; Joseph my son is still alive; I will go and see him before I die (45:28).

insights.title: Revealed to his brothers
insights.body: Joseph, rejected by his brothers, becomes their saviour and reveals himself to them in tears. Stephen draws the parallel with Jesus, rejected by his own.

insights.title: God sent me
insights.body: Joseph saw God at work in his worst experience. Looking back, where has God brought good from something painful in your life?

46.summary: On the way to Egypt, Jacob offers sacrifices at Beersheba, and God tells him not to fear going down, for he will make him a great nation there and bring him back; the seventy members of Jacob's family are listed; Joseph meets his father in Goshen and weeps on his neck.
46.lookfor: Notice God's reassurance, and the reunion of father and son.

names.name: Beersheba
names.gloss: Where Isaac had worshiped God, at the edge of the land.

names.name: Jacob
names.gloss: Leaving Canaan at 130 years old.

names.name: Goshen
names.gloss: The region of Egypt where the family settled.

skim.advice: The middle of the chapter lists Jacob's descendants; skim the names and read the opening and closing scenes.

insights.title: Don't be afraid to go down
insights.body: I am God, the God of your father; don't be afraid to go down into Egypt (46:3). Isaac had been told not to go to Egypt; now God sends Jacob there, with a promise to bring him back.

insights.title: I will go with you
insights.body: I will go down with you into Egypt, and I will also surely bring you up again (46:4). God's presence travels with his people.

insights.title: Seventy
insights.body: All the souls of Jacob's house who came into Egypt were seventy (46:27). As the nations numbered about seventy in chapter 10, Israel begins as seventy, a small world in itself. Stephen's speech, following the Greek text, says seventy-five.

insights.title: He wept on his neck
insights.body: Joseph presented himself to his father, fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a good while (46:29). Twenty-two years of separation end.

insights.title: Now let me die
insights.body: Israel says, now let me die, since I have seen your face (46:30). Like old Simeon holding the infant Jesus: now let your servant depart in peace.

insights.title: Shepherds are abominable
insights.body: Every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians (46:34). Joseph uses this so his family will be settled apart in Goshen, keeping their identity.

insights.title: Into Egypt
insights.body: The family of promise now lives outside the promised land. It sets the stage for Exodus: a great nation, slavery, and a great deliverance.

insights.title: Going down with God
insights.body: God promised to go with Jacob into an unknown land. What unfamiliar place are you facing where you need to know God goes with you?

47.summary: Joseph presents five brothers and his father to Pharaoh, and Jacob blesses Pharaoh; the family settles in the land of Rameses; as famine deepens, Joseph buys all Egypt's land and people for Pharaoh in exchange for grain, setting a fifth as tax; Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan.
47.lookfor: Notice the old shepherd blessing the king, and Jacob's reflection on his life.

names.name: Pharaoh
names.gloss: Who receives Jacob's blessing.

names.name: Goshen
names.gloss: The best of the land, given to Jacob's family.

names.name: Rameses
names.gloss: A region of the delta, named after a later city.

names.name: Jacob
names.gloss: Who lived 147 years.

insights.title: Jacob blessed Pharaoh
insights.body: Jacob blessed Pharaoh (47:7, 47:10). The lesser is blessed by the greater, Hebrews says; here the old shepherd blesses the most powerful man on earth.

insights.title: Few and evil
insights.body: Asked his age, Jacob says, the days of my pilgrimage are 130 years; few and evil have been my days (47:9). An honest, weary summary of a hard life.

insights.title: Rameses
insights.body: The land of Rameses (47:11) is named after a city built much later by Israelite slaves (Exodus 1:11). The writer uses the name his readers knew.

insights.title: Buying Egypt
insights.body: As money and livestock run out, Egyptians sell their land and themselves to Pharaoh for food; Joseph sets a tax of a fifth (47:20-26). Modern readers find this troubling; the people themselves thank Joseph for saving their lives (47:25).

insights.title: Priests exempt
insights.body: Only the priests' land was not bought, because they received an allowance from Pharaoh (47:22). Egyptian temples held vast lands and privileges.

insights.title: Fruitful in Egypt
insights.body: Israel lived in Goshen, acquired property, and was fruitful and multiplied greatly (47:27). The creation blessing comes true even in a foreign land.

insights.title: Bury me with my fathers
insights.body: Jacob makes Joseph swear, with hand under his thigh, not to bury him in Egypt but with his fathers (47:29-30). He trusts the promise of the land.

insights.title: Pilgrimage
insights.body: Jacob called his life a pilgrimage. How does seeing your life as a journey toward God's promise change the way you live today?

48.summary: Jacob, ill, recalls God's promise at Luz, adopts Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh as his own, and blesses them, deliberately crossing his hands to put the younger Ephraim ahead of the older Manasseh, despite Joseph's protest.
48.lookfor: Notice Jacob's crossed hands, and how he describes God in his blessing.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: Joseph's younger son, given the greater blessing.

names.name: Manasseh
names.gloss: Joseph's firstborn son.

names.name: Luz
names.gloss: Bethel's old name, where God appeared to Jacob.

names.name: Rachel
names.gloss: Jacob's beloved wife, buried on the way to Ephrath.

insights.title: Adoption
insights.body: Ephraim and Manasseh, like Reuben and Simeon, will be mine (48:5). By adopting them, Jacob gives Joseph a double portion: two tribes instead of one.

insights.title: I didn't think I'd see your face
insights.body: I didn't think I would see your face, and look, God has let me see your children too (48:11). Grief turned to more than he hoped for.

insights.title: Crossed hands
insights.body: Jacob crosses his arms, putting his right hand on the younger Ephraim (48:14). Once again God's blessing goes to the younger, as with Isaac, Jacob and Joseph himself.

insights.title: The God who shepherded me
insights.body: The God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day, the angel who redeemed me from all evil (48:15-16). Jacob, a shepherd, sees God as his shepherd, the first time the image appears in the Bible.

insights.title: Ephraim and Manasseh
insights.body: In Israel they bless children, may God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh (48:20). Jewish families still say this blessing over sons on Sabbath evenings.

insights.title: God will bring you back
insights.body: I am dying, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers (48:21). The promise will outlive Jacob.

insights.title: A lifelong shepherd
insights.body: Jacob looked back and saw God shepherding him all his life. Looking back over your life, where do you see God's shepherding?

49.summary: Jacob gathers his twelve sons and speaks over each a final word of blessing or judgment that foretells the future of their tribes: Reuben loses his firstborn place, Simeon and Levi are scattered, Judah receives the scepter, and Joseph is richly blessed; Jacob asks to be buried at Machpelah and dies.
49.lookfor: Notice the long blessing on Judah and the promise of the scepter, and the rich blessing on Joseph.

names.name: Reuben
names.gloss: Firstborn, unstable as water.

names.name: Judah
names.gloss: Compared to a lion, given the scepter.

names.name: Zebulun
names.gloss: Who would dwell by the sea.

names.name: Dan
names.gloss: Who would judge his people, like a serpent by the road.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: A fruitful vine by a spring.

names.name: Machpelah
names.gloss: The family tomb near Mamre.

insights.title: Last words
insights.body: Gather together, that I may tell you what will happen to you in the last days (49:1). Deathbed words in the ancient world were taken as prophetic and binding.

insights.title: Reuben, Simeon and Levi
insights.body: Reuben loses preeminence for defiling his father's bed; Simeon and Levi are cursed for their violence (49:3-7). Old sins have long consequences.

insights.title: The lion of Judah
insights.body: Judah is a lion's cub; the scepter won't depart from Judah until he comes to whom it belongs, and to him shall the obedience of the peoples be (49:9-10). Revelation calls Jesus the Lion of the tribe of Judah.

insights.title: Shiloh
insights.body: Until he comes to whom it belongs (49:10). The Hebrew word here, shiloh, is unclear, and older translations kept it as a name, until Shiloh come. Jewish and Christian interpreters have long read it as pointing to the Messiah.

insights.title: Washing in wine
insights.body: He washes his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes (49:11): such abundance that wine is as plentiful as water. A picture of the Messiah's age of plenty.

insights.title: I wait for your salvation
insights.body: In the middle of the blessings, Jacob breaks off: I have waited for your salvation, Yahweh (49:18). A prayer of longing in the midst of prophecy.

insights.title: The Mighty One of Jacob
insights.body: Joseph's blessing names God as the Mighty One of Jacob, the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel (49:24). Joseph's strength came from God's hands.

insights.title: Last words
insights.body: Jacob's last words shaped his family's future. What words would you want to leave with those you love?

50.summary: Joseph mourns his father, and Egypt mourns seventy days; Joseph leads a great procession to bury Jacob in Canaan; afterward his brothers fear revenge, but Joseph weeps and assures them that what they meant for evil, God meant for good; Joseph dies at 110, making Israel promise to carry his bones to the promised land.
50.lookfor: Notice Joseph's response to his brothers' fear, and the hope in his final request.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: Who forgave his brothers and died in Egypt.

names.name: Atad
names.gloss: A threshing floor beyond the Jordan where they mourned.

names.name: Machpelah
names.gloss: Where Jacob was buried with his fathers.

insights.title: Embalming
insights.body: Joseph has physicians embalm his father, taking forty days, and Egypt mourns seventy days (50:2-3). Egyptian mummification is well documented; seventy days was near the length of royal mourning.

insights.title: A great procession
insights.body: Pharaoh's officials, Egypt's elders, chariots and horsemen accompany Jacob's body to Canaan, a very great company (50:7-9). The shepherd is buried like a dignitary.

insights.title: The brothers' fear
insights.body: With Jacob dead, the brothers fear Joseph will now repay them, and send a message, perhaps invented, that their father wanted Joseph to forgive them (50:15-17). Joseph weeps when he hears it.

insights.title: Am I in the place of God?
insights.body: Joseph says, don't be afraid, for am I in the place of God? (50:19). Judgment belongs to God; Joseph refuses to take it.

insights.title: Meant for evil, meant for good
insights.body: You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive (50:20). The key to the whole Joseph story, and one of the clearest statements of providence in the Bible.

insights.title: Carry my bones
insights.body: Joseph makes Israel swear: God will surely visit you, and you shall carry my bones from here (50:25). Moses takes them in the exodus, and they are buried at Shechem.

insights.title: In a coffin in Egypt
insights.body: Genesis ends: they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt (50:26). The book of beginnings ends in a coffin, waiting. Exodus picks up the story.

insights.title: God meant it for good
insights.body: Joseph didn't deny the evil done to him but saw God's purpose over it. What painful event in your life might God use for good?

intro.who: The book doesn't name its author. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses with the first five books (the Torah); many scholars think Genesis was shaped from older sources and completed over centuries, perhaps finished during or after the exile.
intro.when: Its stories run from creation to Joseph's death in Egypt, perhaps around 1600 BC. Tradition dates the writing to Moses' time, around the 1400s or 1200s BC; many scholars place its final form around 500 BC.
intro.why: Genesis means beginnings. It tells how God made a good world, how humanity broke it through sin, and how God began to put it right by choosing one family, Abraham's, through whom all nations would be blessed. It sets up the whole Bible's story.
